content: Decrement tables, also referred to as life tables, are statistical tools used to calculate the probability of specific events occurring over time. In the context of birth control studies, these tables are employed to assess the effectiveness of contraceptive methods. They serve as an alternative to the Pearl Index, which is another commonly used measure of contraceptive efficacy. When applied to birth control research, decrement tables calculate separate effectiveness rates for each month of the study, as well as for a standard time period, typically 12 months. This approach accounts for factors such as the most fertile couples becoming pregnant and leaving the study early, as well as couples improving their proficiency in using the contraceptive method over time. By incorporating these dynamics, decrement tables provide a more nuanced and accurate measure of contraceptive effectiveness compared to the Pearl Index. There are two types of decrement tables used in evaluating birth control methods: multiple-decrement tables and single-decrement tables. Multiple-decrement tables, also known as competing tables, report net effectiveness rates. These are particularly useful for comparing different reasons why couples may drop out of a study. On the other hand, single-decrement tables, or non-competing tables, report gross effectiveness rates. These rates are valuable for making accurate comparisons between different studies. For further reading, refer to works such as The Art of Natural Family Planning by John Kippley (1996), which discusses these methods in detail, and various studies by Trussell and colleagues that analyze contraceptive failure and efficacy using decrement and life table techniques.
